title: Making Your Rivals Dependent on Your System Is America's Three-Hundred-Year Winning Secret
dek: The Dutch, British, and Americans took turns as top dog not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake everything on their maritime system—once they can't live without your shipping lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective killer short of war.
why: Walter Mead breaks down America's three hundred years of success into a five-step strategy, extending it to China, the Taiwan Strait, and AI deterrence. He offers a durable framework for judgment, not news-driven opinions.
who: Overseas founders and those in China-US supply chains, engineers studying the Taiwan Strait or drone warfare transformation, and investors focused on AI policy risk.

points.h: Unpredictability Is a Form of Power
points.body: ‘Unpredictability’ is not madness but a modern power strategy. Mead says post-Cold War US diplomacy relied on ‘letting the world know where America's red lines are’ as a pillar of stability, but Trump profits from the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age—the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. Clinton, besieged by the Lewinsky scandal, discovered that shame lives only in others' minds; as long as you keep moving forward, the dogs bark but the caravan passes. Trump scaled this insight to industrial proportions. The cost is borne by the US diplomatic system: when the world's top power itself becomes the unpredictable card, the alliances and rules built on predictability since World War II accelerate their unraveling.

points.h: The Final Step of Global Hegemony Is Cutting Off
points.body: The Anglo-American maritime order won not through a single battle but a five-step playbook: first, open societies on islands—17th-century Holland tolerated heretics and Jews, attracting thought and capital; then global trade, Dutch merchant ships spanning the world, wealth so abundant that paintings featured Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over Silesia inland, you grabbed India and Canada globally. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of Spain's colonial blockade, invite everyone in to do business—the British navy fought pirates, benefiting all merchant ships; Germany and Japan were similarly welcomed after their wars. The final step is the trump card: once rivals depend on your grain, rubber, and shipping lanes, cut them off—Germany in WWI suddenly found Argentine grain and Malayan rubber cut off, and its economy collapsed.

points.h: All of China's Efforts Are About Preventing the Umbilical Cord from Being Cut
points.body: Viewing China through the same framework, one sees Beijing is acutely aware of its vulnerability. Mead says, suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from 100 miles off Taiwan's coast: oil can't come in, manufactured goods can't go out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided—China's economy would be strangled. He has discussed these scenarios with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this concern is always present. So China's energy policy should be read in parallel: building oil reserves on a scale that surprises outsiders, while aggressively expanding solar and hydro, and mining as much coal as possible. It's not schizophrenia but one thing: plucking out, one by one, the weaknesses of ‘dependence on the outside world.’ He also warns America against retreating into isolationism—agriculture and AI need overseas markets to sustain themselves.

points.h: Each Technological Dividend Needs New Institutions
points.body: Mead starts with the ownership society: at America's founding, land was held by independent farmers; building a bridge might be good but would raise my taxes—that trade-off itself was political education. The railroad era paired with the Homestead Act, where the government gave land to railroad companies and farmers, growing a national market; in the 20th century, the suburban single-family home replaced the family farm, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth distribution machine. Today that machine hits housing prices: young people can't afford to live near work. His remedies are remote work and autonomous driving. Commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, and available housing land grows with the square of the radius—the physical space technology opens can support another two generations. But the prerequisite is institutional ‘infrastructure’—he coined the term info-structure, meaning the institutional and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

points.h: Silicon Valley Tilts Toward Tech Hamiltonianism
points.body: American foreign policy debates for centuries have been four schools: Hamiltonian wants a strong state to clear the way for capital, Wilsonian wants to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonian fears big government, and Jacksonian is isolationist in peacetime but hits back hard when attacked. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamiltonian and Wilsonian, but Trump brought Jeffersonian and Jacksonian into play. Mead says the truly notable new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s, tech companies liked to say ‘we're a global company, Google has no borders, Washington can't touch us’; AI competition turned tech into a matter of national destiny. Economic stances changed too: old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply chain and IP security, even hoping employees are patriotic—selling code to China is shameful, and colleagues will report you. The commercial core shifting from old multinationals to tech nationalists is the underwater current of American political realignment.

points.h: The More Equipped the Power, the More It Fears Technological Generational Shifts
points.body: Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later, progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually with only two or three soldiers operating together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to evacuate the wounded’—you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people out, accompanied by a swarm of hunter drones to kill enemy drones attacking yours. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front line. Changes flip every six months. The irony for America: the power with the most tanks and carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this parameter revolution—existing equipment goes from advantage to sunk cost. The Russian Black Sea Fleet has no major battles to fight, yet is trapped at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

points.h: The New Variable to Watch in the Taiwan Strait Is Japan
points.body: On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment: Beijing needs a very high probability of success to cross the threshold—failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ lies a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade—actions that change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The truly new variable on the Taiwan chessboard is not the US attitude but Japan. The Japanese have publicly stated that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is over; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrines, and reshaping national psychology. Historically, Japan has turned quickly when facing real threats. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must include the Japan factor, will be the key to the Taiwan issue in the coming years.

points.h: AI Actually Makes Deterrence More Credible
points.body: Applying Cold War deterrence logic to the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive conclusion: deterrence succeeds when the opponent is 100% certain that ‘if I do X, you will inevitably do Y, and you can and will do it.’ As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain—‘I might soften at that moment’—the commitment has a crack. Automating part of diplomatic decisions to AI turns retaliation into an executable, hesitation-free mechanism—deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine dilemma of science fiction: decisions of annihilation no longer require humans to bear the consequences. His own assessment is ‘very interesting and somewhat puzzling,’ and he does not think an answer has emerged.

terms.def: A new force in US foreign policy advocating state power to pave the way for tech companies, replacing old free-market multinational capital.
The institutional, legal, and regulatory frameworks needed for AI to safely land in hospitals, courts, and other settings—distinct from physical infrastructure.
The American hawkish tradition of staying out of foreign affairs in peacetime but using overwhelming force to destroy enemies when attacked.
A pressure tactic that strangles an adversary's trade gradually through customs, insurance, and port rules rather than direct warfare.
